```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8.0,
  fig.height = 4.6,
  dpi = 120
)
library(rgraphtool)
```

This article reproduces and extends the classic ecological case study from the
[`sbm` R package](https://grosssbm.github.io/sbm/) (`fungusTreeNetwork`,
originating from Vacher, Piou & Desprez-Loustau 2008, *PLoS ONE* 3(3): e1740)
using `rgraphtool`'s native C++23 microcanonical Bipartite Stochastic Block
Model (Yen & Larremore 2020) and weighted edge-covariate SBMs (Peixoto 2018).

The bundled dataset `fungus_tree_network()` records antagonistic interactions
between **154 fungal species** and **51 European tree species**, along with the
projected $51 \times 51$ tree--tree shared-fungus count matrix and pairwise
genetic, taxonomic, and geographic distances between trees.

## 1. Inspecting the fungus--tree network

`fungus_tree_network()` returns both the raw matrices and a validated
`rgraphtool_graph` with vertex `"type"` (`FALSE` for fungi, `TRUE` for trees)
and `"name"` property maps:

```{r load-data}
ft <- fungus_tree_network()
dim(ft$fungus_tree)
sum(ft$fungus_tree)

ft$graph
is_bipartite(ft$graph)
```

## 2. Fitting a microcanonical Bipartite SBM

Just like `sbm::estimateBipartiteSBM()`, `minimize_bipartite_blockmodel_dl()`
accepts a rectangular incidence matrix directly (or a `bipartite_graph()`
object). Rather than requiring a grid search over block numbers with variational
EM, `rgraphtool` minimizes the exact microcanonical bipartite description length
$\Sigma$ in C++23—using the bipartite edge-count prior
$\ln\binom{B_{\text{fungus}} B_{\text{tree}} + E - 1}{E}$ to select
$(B_{\text{fungus}}, B_{\text{tree}})$ automatically without resolution-limit
penalties from impossible intra-type edges:

```{r fit-bipartite, fig.height = 4.8}
set.seed(42)
fit_bip <- minimize_bipartite_blockmodel_dl(
  ft$fungus_tree,
  dim_labels = c("fungus", "tree"),
  nruns = 3L
)
fit_bip

# Separate 1-based block memberships for fungi and trees (with species names)
mem <- bipartite_membership(fit_bip)
table(fungus_block = mem$fungus)
table(tree_block = mem$tree)

# Rectangular B_fungus x B_tree interaction density matrix
round(bipartite_block_matrix(fit_bip, normalize = "density"), 3)

# Reordered incidence matrix ("data" view) and mesoscale block diagram ("meso" view)
old_par <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1L, 2L), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot_bipartite(fit_bip, type = "matrix", main = "Reordered incidence matrix")
plot_bipartite(fit_bip, type = "meso", main = "Mesoscale fungus-tree blocks")
graphics::par(old_par)
```

## 3. Degree correction, hierarchy & Bayesian posterior sampling

Ecological interaction networks typically exhibit pronounced degree
heterogeneity (generalist vs. specialist species). `compare_bipartite_models()`
compares degree-corrected (DC) vs. non-degree-corrected (NDC) and flat vs.
hierarchical (nested) bipartite SBMs by exact description length:

```{r compare-and-sample}
set.seed(42)
cmp <- compare_bipartite_models(
  ft$fungus_tree,
  dim_labels = c("fungus", "tree"),
  nruns = 2L
)
cmp

# Finite-temperature MCMC posterior sampling around the MAP bipartite state
set.seed(42)
post <- sample_posterior(fit_bip, nsamples = 50L, burnin = 25L, thin = 2L)
summary(post$entropies)
```

## 4. Simple & covariate-weighted SBMs on the tree--tree network

Following the second half of the `GrossSBM/sbm` tutorial, we also analyze the
unipartite $51 \times 51$ `tree_tree` network (counting how many fungal
parasites each pair of tree species shares), comparing a binary topology SBM, a
Poisson count SBM (`discrete-poisson`), and a multi-covariate SBM incorporating
taxonomic distance (`covar_tree$taxonomic_dist`):

```{r tree-tree-sbm}
tree_mat <- ft$tree_tree
diag(tree_mat) <- 0
idx <- which(upper.tri(tree_mat) & tree_mat > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)

g_tree <- graph_create(nrow(tree_mat), directed = FALSE)
graph_set_vertex_property(g_tree, "name", ft$tree_names)
graph_add_edges(
  g_tree,
  idx,
  properties = list(
    shared_fungi = tree_mat[idx],
    genetic_dist = ft$covar_tree$genetic_dist[idx],
    taxonomic_dist = ft$covar_tree$taxonomic_dist[idx],
    geographic_dist = ft$covar_tree$geographic_dist[idx]
  )
)
g_tree

set.seed(42)
fit_tree_bin <- minimize_blockmodel_dl(g_tree)
fit_tree_poi <- minimize_weighted_blockmodel_dl(
  g_tree, weights = "shared_fungi", types = "discrete-poisson"
)
fit_tree_cov <- minimize_weighted_blockmodel_dl(
  g_tree,
  weights = c("shared_fungi", "taxonomic_dist"),
  types = c("discrete-poisson", "real-exponential")
)

cat(sprintf("Binary tree SBM: %d blocks (DL = %.2f nats)\n",
            length(block_sizes(fit_tree_bin)),
            block_description_length(fit_tree_bin)))
print(fit_tree_poi)
print(fit_tree_cov)
```

## 5. Exporting & round-tripping with `graph-tool` (`.gt`) and `igraph`

Because `bipartite_graph()` stores `"type"` and `"name"` as standard vertex
property maps and `"dim_labels"` as a graph property map, bipartite networks
round-trip losslessly through both Python `graph-tool`'s binary `.gt` format and
R's `igraph` package:

```{r io-roundtrip}
gt_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".gt.gz")
write_gt(ft$graph, gt_path)
g_reloaded <- read_gt(gt_path)
unlink(gt_path)

identical(as_incidence_matrix(g_reloaded), ft$fungus_tree)

if (requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ig <- as_igraph(ft$graph)
  cat(sprintf("igraph bipartite: %s (%d vertices, %d edges)\n",
              igraph::is_bipartite(ig), igraph::vcount(ig), igraph::ecount(ig)))
  g_from_ig <- bipartite_graph(ig)
  identical(as_incidence_matrix(g_from_ig), ft$fungus_tree)
}
```

## References

- Vacher, C., Piou, D., & Desprez-Loustau, M.-L. (2008). Architecture of an
  antagonistic tree/fungus network: the asymmetric influence of past
  evolutionary history. *PLoS ONE*, 3(3), e1740.
- Yen, T.-C., & Larremore, D. B. (2020). Community detection in bipartite
  networks with stochastic block models. *Physical Review E*, 102(3), 032309.
- Chiquet, J., Donnet, S., & Barbillon, P. (`GrossSBM/sbm`): *Stochastic
  Blockmodels* R package (<https://grosssbm.github.io/sbm/>).
